title: Wonder and discovery
hook: the Granth's wonder at countless worlds sits easily with curiosity

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Japji's last salok: air the Guru, water the father, earth the great mother. Your line was the great mother. What bit of earth did you care for? Day one thousand three hundred ninety.

Worlds below worlds. Skies above skies. That's how one verse of the Japji opens, and it keeps going: people have searched and searched to the very edge, and grown tired, and the edge is still not found. If the count could be written down, it would be. But the writing runs out first. And the Granth's response to a creation too big to measure isn't fear, or a closed door. It's a word the Gurus come back to with delight. Today's word is that response.
screen: `WORLDS BELOW WORLDS. SKIES ABOVE SKIES.` → `THE WRITING RUNS OUT FIRST.` → `NOT FEAR. DELIGHT.`

segments.voice: First, the word. Vismaad means wonder, awe, the astonished stillness that comes when something is bigger than your mind can hold. It isn't confusion. It's being overwhelmed in the right direction. Second, the Japji's map. In the verse we heard, Guru Nanak describes creation as layered past counting, and says plainly that it can't be fully written down. That's not a ban on looking. It's an honest note about scale: however far you go, there's farther. Third, the wonder hymn. In Asa di Var, Guru Nanak lets the word ring again and again. In paraphrase: wonder the sound, wonder the Vedas, the books of knowledge; wonder the creatures, wonder their kinds; wonder the forms, wonder the colors; wonder the wind, wonder the water, wonder the fire at play; wonder the near, wonder the far. Notice what sits in that list. The books of knowledge stand right beside the wind and the fire. Learning isn't the end of wonder there. It's one of the wonders. Fourth, curiosity. Some people fear that learning how the world works will drain the awe out of it. The Granth's picture runs the other way. The more you see, the more there is to be astonished by. A Sikh astronomer, or a child with a microscope, isn't trespassing on the sacred. They're doing vismaad with better instruments. Discovery doesn't close the book. It turns a page and finds the book is bigger than you thought. That's why the line for today is not wonder stops learning, but the opposite.
screen: `VISMAAD: AWE PAST WHAT THE MIND HOLDS.` · `JAPJI: WORLDS PAST COUNTING.` · `ASA DI VAR: EVEN KNOWLEDGE IS A WONDER.` · `DISCOVERY TURNS THE PAGE.` · then, large: `WONDER KEEPS LEARNING.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: learn one fact about space. Before the bell, or after it, look up one thing: the name of the nearest star after the sun, what a nebula is, why Mars is red. Now settle, and breathe. Hold the fact gently, the way you'd hold something fragile. Breathe in, and let it be large. Breathe out, and notice whether the bigness feels like a threat or a gift. If you can, let the word come quietly with the out-breath: vismaad. The bell holds the time.
Vismaad. Wonder, awe, the astonished stillness before a creation too big to hold; in Asa di Var, even the books of knowledge are among the wonders. Today's word.
Your line: wonder keeps learning. Today, tell someone the fact you learned, and see if a little vismaad travels with it. Day one thousand three hundred ninety.

howItsDone: Sikhs speak of vismaad as the awe the Gurus describe before creation; the Japji's verse on worlds below and skies above is part of the daily morning prayer.

original.note: Gurmukhi: vismaad, wonder and awe, the word that rings through Guru Nanak's wonder hymn in Asa di Var.

trapdoor: what you thought: wonder is what you feel before you understand.
what it means: vismaad is awe that keeps growing as you learn more.
what a scholar hears: Asa di Var lists the books of knowledge among the wonders, and the Japji says the writing runs out before creation's count.

sources.ref: Ang 463–464 (Asa di Var, salok of Guru Nanak: 'vismad naad vismad ved')

notes: Please confirm Japji pauri 22 (Ang 5) and the paraphrase; the Gurmukhi gives large numbers (lakh), which the script renders as 'past counting' to avoid stating a count.
Please confirm the Ang for the 'vismad naad vismad ved' salok and the paraphrase of its list, including 'wonder is the knowing' (vismad giaan).
The hook says the verse was sung 'long before anyone pointed a telescope' at a galaxy; this is general, please check it's acceptable.
'A Sikh astronomer ... doing vismaad with better instruments' is an image, not a claim about any person.
The practice's example questions are invitations; the script states no astronomical fact.

Editor: removed 'wonder is the knowing' (no 'vismad giaan' in the salok); the line now rests on 'vismad ved', glossed as the Vedas, the books of knowledge, across teach, word and games; cut the telescope comparison (a dating claim that implies prescience).
